speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I will speak on the issue of taxes on capital because such taxes matter not only for the sustainability of our public purse, but also because their just application could reshape the landscape of rising inequality in income and wealth, matters which matter enormously to the common man and woman.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My speech will first lay out the case for and against taxes on capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will then explain why our Government's revenue mix can potentially benefit from attention to a richer slate of objectives and how wealth taxes can play a role in meeting those expanded objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will then discuss a menu of possible taxes on capital, before closing with a specific proposal for wealth taxation in the modern world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will begin by declaring that I am the Chief Economist (Emeritus) of Thirdrock Group, a homegrown asset and wealth management advisory, and am still occasionally invited to speak at various academic and industry events to audiences that serve high networth individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is useful to clarify, first, what I mean when I speak of taxes on capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a tax applied to any form of productive assets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most common form is the corporate income tax levied on profits for a company.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another common form are allowances for expenditure on plant and machinery; and since these are write-offs, they are negative capital taxes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Truth be told, discussion on capital taxes seldom focus on these routine forms, which are widespread and uncontentious.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, they centre either on capital gains taxes, which are applied to receipts through the ownership or sale of financial property, or intangible assets, along with wealth taxes, which are charged to the outstanding value of an individual's assets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the issue of capital gains is important, it is best left for another day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, I will only focus on wealth taxes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most common objection to capital taxes in general is that this entails a double taxation of income, since capital holdings typically result from saved income, which had already been taxed previously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we can still make the case for a separate taxation of capital if we accept that taxes are always due whenever they are productive gains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In such instances, taxes reflect a host of indirect benefits, such as a well-functioning legal system and financial infrastructure or initial tax breaks the individuals and firms receive when they first invest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since the risks of providing such benefits are borne by society, it is reasonable to recoup these after gains are realised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another common objection is that taxes applied to wealth may be excessive because by eroding the principal, it could kill the very goose that laid the golden eggs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, there is actually little difference in principle between taxes on the flow of profits versus the stock of wealth so long as the latter also generates income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MOF has often stated that it maintains a diverse revenue mix to finance its Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a broad range of contributions is important because it ensures that Government spending needs are not threatened by declines in any single source.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In that sense, the revenue mix has a certain robustness and resilience built into it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: From another perspective, however, this revenue mix is rather imbalanced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While our overall tax system may be progressive – that is, the effects are felt more keenly by the rich than the poor – a quarter of our taxes remain regressive, even with the current Voucher Scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, fees and charges, especially the fines that our little red dot is so infamous for, also hit the poor disproportionately harder than the rich.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, there is no correct revenue mix when it comes to financing Government expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, we can aim for objectives that go beyond efficient collection and diverse sources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, one laudable objective is that we should seek to minimise, as much as possible, the number of regressive components in the tax regime rather than just being content that the system happens to be progressive overall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Recent global developments also make the case that the time is ripe to re-examine our traditional tax mix.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is where wealth taxes come into play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such taxes will shore up the diversity of our revenue sources, especially the contribution from capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Wealth taxes also offer an additional potential benefit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is a tool that can help reduce the overall level of inequality in society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Why should we care about disparities in income and wealth?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For economic, social and moral reasons, therefore, countries cannot afford to allow inequality to continue its inexorable rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, is inequality in income and wealth a problem in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most popular measure of inequality is known as the Gini coefficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This metric captures in a single number the extent to which existing distribution of income or wealth departs from the theoretical ideal of perfect equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The higher the number, the more unequal the distribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because different countries scale this coefficient differently, a direct comparison between countries is challenging but not impossible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This implies that pandemic-related assistance and tax relief, which surged in 2020, was responsible for the improvement in equality outcomes rather than any disproportionate drop in income from the rich.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other metrics of income inequality tell a similar story.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, despite the massive drop of close to 6% of gross domestic product (GDP) growth last year, household wealth actually went in the opposite direction, expanding by around 15%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notably, this wealth Gini at 0.783 by one estimate is much higher than that of comparable neighbouring economies such as Japan, Korea or Taiwan.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, these facts suggest that inequality is a real and pressing issue and our nation's effort at redistribution has been far more restrained than in other advanced economies, including that of our immediate neighbours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can do more to address our inequality problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Between 1929 and 2008, Singapore taxed inheritance via an estate duty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Estate Duty Act was amended in 2005 to apply only to estates of those that passed prior to 15 February 2008.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: During the debate on the abolition, Members explained that wealth was now being generated by other means, thereby rendering the inheritance less impactful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The duty was also viewed as a tax that affected mostly the middle class as the wealthy had generally been able to shelter the estates from such taxes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Stamp duties and Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) are also currently applied to properties in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Buyer's Stamp Duty is applied progressively up to a marginal rate of 4% for property values in excess of $1 million.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: ABSD is payable on additional properties and by most non-Singaporeans and it is likewise progressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Both taxes play triple duty by not just raising revenue and enhancing progressivity, but also by helping contain speculative pressure, especially from wealthy international buyers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The major strategic reason for eliminating taxes on inheritance was to provide greater ballast for Singapore as it sought to position itself as a globally competitive wealth management centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The fear is that in reintroducing an estate duty, even a limited one, could weaken our value proposition as a wealth centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may also seem unnecessary, given the small amounts that will be raised by the reintroduction of such a tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or we could weave in greater progressivity into our estate duty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The top marginal tax rate for properties above $1 million is currently set at 4%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We could introduce another tier for higher value properties – at 5% for properties valued above $5 million or for owners of multiple properties that cumulatively exceed $5 million.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The suggestion was recently raised by my Sengkang GRC colleague, Louis Chua, in his speech to this House on the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As he shared, with a relatively high threshold, the aspiring middle class would not be penalised by such a tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This option has the additional benefit of tempering increases in house prices even in public housing because private housing prices have a spillover effect on public markets in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or, alternatively, we could introduce a progressive net worth tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While wealth taxes could, in principle, be applied to any amount of asset holdings, most proponents have in mind only the highest tier of wealthy individuals such as those in the top 1% or, more likely, in the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The wealth tax can itself be progressive with different marginal rates for various income tiers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The key advantage of such wealth taxes is that it ensures that the large and growing asset basis of ultra-high net worth individuals, which is typically held in non-property form, would not be inadvertently exempt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In choosing the target tax base, we should strike a balance between raising revenue and effecting redistribution versus heightening the incentives for avoidance and evasion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One way to minimise evasion is to make such taxes one-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, one-off taxes are best when there is no prior announcement since doing so will impose the least distortion due to tax avoidance behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, sudden major policy announcements are seldom infeasible in the real world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, the significant amount of work in the run-up to implementation, legislative design, asset valuation, collection mechanisms will only be drawn on once.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Any revenue gain, redistributed benefits and impact on inequality will also be temporary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A practical solution to this is to require one-off assessment but have payments rendered over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another strategy to limit evasions is allow the wealthy some agency in the deployment of their tax contributions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, a wealth tax could be directed to foundations, which by mandate will be required to spend a fixed amount of the endowment each year on approved causes until depleted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, the tax can be levied annually and collected amounts automatically channelled to the foundation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, legal instruments such as charitable trusts or foundations already exist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All that is required is for us to pair the wealth tax with these entities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This tax should be designed in a manner that takes into account current realities, including the inherent mobility of capital and wealth but also the importance of not just taxes but other non-monetary motivations for why high net worth individuals may choose Singapore as a home for asset and wealth management.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We could even permit tax loss harvesting for up to two years or restrict taxation to only instances where net wealth gains are positive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In either case, the returns on wealth in any given year would typically significantly exceed these tax rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, they should get rid of their wealth manager.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the ultra-rich should generally not expect to see any decrease in the principal on the asset.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The natural reservation to doing so would be that it would threaten our competitive position as a global wealth management centre, especially relative to our closest competitors, Hong Kong and Switzerland.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: International developments have also pointed to a greater appetite for cross-country cooperation on tax regimes, such as the OECD deal on the global corporate taxes I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is therefore not inconceivable that similar agreements on wealth taxation could be in the offing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, we need to disabuse ourselves from the mistaken notion that low taxes offer the most competitive advantage for our status as a global financial centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tax competition is a mindset more suited for the 20th, rather than the 21st century.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We already have experience with other forms of wealth taxation in the past, and we need not fear the competitive position for the future, because other jurisdictions have already moved ahead with similar taxes on capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Gotham was dank, crime-ridden and deeply unequal, but Mr Wayne, like his philanthropic father before him, chose to expend his own enormous wealth to redress the very imbalance that he had been such a beneficiary of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My heartfelt belief is that all of us, the ultra-wealthy included, want to live in a world where we can all contribute our fair share to make it a better place, both today and for our children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is how I view wealth taxes: it is another salve for our imperfect world, an opportunity to create new opportunities for Singaporeans, and an idea whose time has come.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What we have in Singapore today is one of the most progressive system of taxes and transfers in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is possible because we have a competitive, fair and sustainable tax system, painstakingly built up by the Government over the years, which not only raises revenue, but keeps our economy dynamic, builds an inclusive society and enables a greener future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, real income has grown over the years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The redistribution in taxes is done pursuant to our goal for a fair society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This compares favourably with other jurisdictions, such as the UK and Finland, where middle-income households receive only $1.25 of benefits for every dollar of tax paid.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It keeps the tax burden on our people and businesses low, letting them retain most of what they earn.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It keeps the economy dynamic and thus creates good jobs for our people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is not easy to keep the overall tax burden low, as any Government will tell you.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we have been able to do so because we manage our spending effectively and get as much value as we can out of the tax dollars collected for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have achieved good outcomes in many areas, including healthcare and education, for every dollar of spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Perhaps most uniquely of all, we have the Net Investment Return Contribution (NIRC) to supplement our revenue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The NIRC is already our largest revenue source – around 3% of GDP in revenue a year on average and in fact, for every dollar we spend, 20 cents comes from our NIRC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Because of NIRC, Singaporeans pay lower taxes than they would otherwise have to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is unlike many developed countries which, not having something like the NIRC, have to borrow to meet their spending needs and use tax revenues worth 2-3% of GDP each year to service their national debt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In addition, we have the reserves as a failsafe in times of crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is where our tax system is today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we cannot and will not stand still.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are continuously reviewing our tax system, not only to meet the needs of today but the challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have many but these are the three most pressing, structural ones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: About one in four will be 65 and above by the end of this decade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We can expect Government healthcare spending to rise significantly, from 2.2% of GDP in 2019 to 3% of our GDP by 2030.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Three percent of GDP is comparable to what we currently spend, as a proportion of GDP, on defence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must redouble our efforts to make sustainable investments to green our economy and mitigate the impact of climate change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Protecting our coastlines against rising sea levels alone will cost about $100 billion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This means more investments to reduce inequality and promote social mobility, for instance, in building more preschools and improving opportunities for lifelong education.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Yet, even as our structural spending needs continue to increase, our revenue streams are becoming increasingly uncertain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our investment returns from our NIRC will face significant headwinds in a more challenging global investment environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Global tax developments under the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting, or BEPS, will have an uncertain impact on our tax revenue streams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But whatever we do must strike the right balance among raising sufficient revenue, maintaining competitiveness and progressivity, and being sustainable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have a concrete revenue plan to achieve this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have already made some changes and have announced others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, we have continually been raising and enhancing the progressivity of our income taxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also tax wealth and have been raising asset-related taxes like property tax, stamp duty and additional registration fees for higher-end cars or residential property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, we are currently reviewing the carbon tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will update at next year's Budget the carbon tax level for 2024 and what can be expected up to 2030.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, we have indicated the need to raise the GST rate sometime between 2022 and 2025, subject to economic outlook.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will raise revenues of around 0.7% of our GDP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But even as we raise the GST rate, we are committed to cushioning the impact for Singaporean households, including the middle-income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, I think, has focused today on wealth taxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Broadly, we are not in disagreement in the sense that we are constantly looking for ways to be able to supplement our revenue but to do that in a way that strikes the right balance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, on wealth taxes, it is not about having more types of wealth taxes per se.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Rather, what matters is having wealth tax policies that work in the context of each jurisdiction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Take, for example, Switzerland, which has a net wealth tax, estate duty and property-related tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In total, their wealth tax revenue is about 1.9% of GDP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is comparable to Singapore's wealth tax revenue at about 1.8% of our GDP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The question has never been one of whether we want to tax wealth but a practical one, of how to do so effectively such that it cannot be avoided easily.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the end of the day, I think we do not have any issue with wealth taxes per say.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We just want to make sure that whatever we put in place actually works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think the Member suggested that companies may no longer look at the tax rates and that it is not one of the factors that they take into account.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But it is not something that can be discounted completely because businesses and individuals will still look at tax rates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It must be remembered that wealth can move.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Talent, both Singaporean as well as foreign, can move.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, we have to tax in a way that is competitive; that allows people and companies to generate revenue in order to encourage them to stay here; and that revenue can then be used, reallocated and redistributed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Just one last point – the Member spoke about GST and said that it affects the lower- and middle-income disproportionately more.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think that is something, a line, which the Workers' Party repeats very often.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That standalone line in itself is fair enough.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But what must always accompany that line, and I do hope the Assoc Prof Lim and his colleagues will remember, the accompanying balance to that line is that in Singapore, the way we have designed our GST system is that we tilt it more in favour of helping the middle-income and the lower-income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When talking about GST, one must not talk about the impact on middle-income and lower-income alone but to be fair, it is very important to also look at what we do to support and buffer the middle- and lower-income in order to take away any of the additional burden that falls on them as a result of GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In that way, we make it a fairer system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is also fair across generations and can withstand the test of time It is dynamic as it places a low tax burden on workers and businesses and allows them to retain the fruits of their labour.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We care about competitiveness not for the sake of competitiveness but to promote growth for the benefit of all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is what a well-designed 21st century tax system should look like and we will continue to refine it to make it even better.
